subject: Climate & Environment
title: How Wind Turbines Work
description: A 60-second lesson on How Wind Turbines Work.

hook.text: Wind is just air molecules moving from high pressure to low pressure. Turbines harvest that motion.

buildup.text: Blades are shaped like airplane wings. Moving air creates lift that spins the rotor.

discovery.text: The spinning rotor turns a generator inside the nacelle, converting motion into electricity.

twist.text: Turbines can only capture about 59% of wind energy. This is called the Betz limit.

climax.text: Modern turbines hit 45-50% efficiency — close to the theoretical maximum.

punchline.text: Wind pushes a wing, a wing spins a magnet, and lights turn on.

quiz.question: What is the Betz limit?
options: The maximum energy a turbine can extract from wind (~59%)
The tallest a turbine can be built

details.summary: Wind turbines convert kinetic energy from moving air into electricity. Wind spins blades connected to a rotor, which turns a generator inside the nacelle. Modern onshore turbines can reach 200 meters tall and generate enough power for thousands of homes each.
details.whyItMatters: Wind energy is one of the cheapest and fastest-growing sources of clean electricity. Understanding turbine mechanics helps assess its scalability and limitations.
takeaways: Blades capture wind's kinetic energy and spin a generator
Modern turbines can exceed 200 meters in total height
A single large turbine can power several thousand homes

faq.question: Why do wind turbines have three blades?
faq.answer: Three blades offer the best balance of efficiency, stability, and cost. Fewer blades spin faster and create more stress, while more blades add weight and cost without significant efficiency gains. Three blades also produce smoother rotation.

faq.question: What is the maximum energy a turbine can capture?
faq.answer: The Betz limit states that no turbine can capture more than 59.3 percent of wind's kinetic energy. Modern turbines achieve 35 to 45 percent efficiency, approaching theoretical limits while accounting for real-world losses.
